section_title: Why does sharing the good news matter?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 14 How then can they call on the One in whom they have not believed? And how can they believe in the One of whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without someone to preach? 15 And how can they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!” 16 But not all of them welcomed the good news. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed our message?” 17 Consequently, faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ.

context_lines: Paul follows the promise about calling on the Lord with a chain of questions. Calling depends on believing; believing involves hearing; hearing requires a messenger; and the messenger must be sent. Proclaiming the good news belongs within the way people come to faith.

He quotes Isaiah’s welcome for a bearer of good news, then Isaiah’s question about who has believed the report. Sending and hearing do not mean everyone welcomes what is announced. Paul holds the need for proclamation beside the reality of unbelief.
Verse 17 connects faith with hearing and hearing with the word of Christ. The focus is the message about Him, rather than the messenger’s status or ability to impress an audience.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read this as a strong reason to proclaim the gospel: people need to hear the message of Christ in order to respond in faith. The passage also recognizes that hearing a message and welcoming it are different. It does not promise that every presentation will produce an immediate conversion.
god_plan_lines: [Isaiah 52:7–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/52.htm) pictures good news arriving in Zion: God reigns, comforts His people and makes His salvation known to the nations. Paul brings that messenger picture into the proclamation of Christ.

He also draws on [Isaiah 53:1–3](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/53.htm), where the report meets disbelief and the servant is despised. The two quotations hold together the greatness of God’s saving news and the painful possibility of its rejection. Faithful proclamation belongs to God’s work even when its reception is difficult.
